title: Research tips from SYSK
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck open with a listener mail from Bianca about research misrepresentation, unpublished negative studies, and preregistration, then work through a HowStuffWorks article, "Ten signs that study is bogus." Points covered include unrepeatable results (Center for Open Science reproducibility project), plausible-but-unproven observational studies and chance correlations, media overhyping of initial findings, unsound samples and WEIRD study participants, small sample sizes and statistical power, pressure on trainees, dropping inconvenient data, predatory publishing and fake journals, follow-the-money funding conflicts (Willie Soon), fake peer review (Dr. Moon), and sensational "cool story" science reporting. The episode closes with an "Administrative Details" segment thanking listeners for gifts and a sign-off.

segments.title: Cold open and listener mail setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode and say they will open with a listener mail from Bianca about research misrepresentation and selective publication of studies.

segments.title: Ten signs a study is bogus: unrepeatable results and plausibility
segments.summary: Chuck introduces a HowStuffWorks article on spotting bogus studies. Signs discussed include sensational headlines with no follow-up, and the Center for Open Science project in which researchers tried to reproduce one hundred psychological studies and found more than half could not be reproduced. The hosts also discuss plausible-but-unprovable observational studies, the type A personality and heart attack example, and chance correlations at the five percent level.

segments.title: Media hype and unsound samples
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the media portrays tentative findings as certain, citing a Mayan city discovery story. They then cover unsound samples, such as a study on first sexual experience that interviewed only college students and heterosexuals and excluded people reporting violent encounters.

segments.title: WEIRD study participants and small sample sizes
segments.summary: The hosts explain the WEIRD acronym (Western, educated, industrialized, rich, democratic) and a survey finding that about eighty percent of social science papers used college student participants. They then discuss small sample sizes and statistical power using a smoking and lung cancer example.

segments.title: Funding pressure, trainees, and data exclusion
segments.summary: Ulrich Dirnagl is cited as a crusader for good science and co-author of a Nature article on institutional responsibility for reproducibility. A survey of MD Anderson trainees found nearly a third felt pressure to support their mentors' work. The hosts discuss a stroke drug study in which mice deaths were dropped from the results, and the pressure to bury negative results.

segments.title: Predatory publishing and fake journals
segments.summary: The hosts describe predatory publishers that charge authors fees after accepting papers. Jeffrey Beall's list of predatory publishers is mentioned, along with fake journals such as Scientific Journals International and an invented award. The hosts link the problem to open-access journals and Aaron Swartz.

segments.title: Follow the money: funding conflicts and climate change denial
segments.summary: The hosts advise following funding sources. They discuss physicist Willie Soon, who denies human-caused climate change, received about 1.2 million dollars from energy companies and foundations, and did not disclose the conflicts. The Heartland Institute gave him an award, and the hosts mention its past work with Philip Morris on secondhand smoke.

segments.title: Fake peer review and initial findings
segments.summary: The hosts describe Dr. Moon, who posed as his own peer reviewers using invented email addresses and was caught when reviews returned too quickly. A Berlin publisher had sixty-four retractions from fraudulent reviews. The hosts then discuss how initial findings get reported as settled science.

segments.title: Cool stories sell science
segments.summary: The hosts argue that media wants a catchy story more than sound science, and joke about sensational claims. They end the discussion of science reporting.

segments.title: Administrative Details and outro
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck thank listeners for gifts including coffee, handmade bowls, pasta, cards, cookies, a book from Rocky Mountain Institute, and 3D-printed items. They give social media contacts and the website, then sign off.
